title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Government data is biased

Rebuttal: Agencies like Census and BLS use transparent methods and are relied on by businesses and both parties. Disagree with policy, not with measurement.

Sources: Census, BLS

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The rich pay most federal income taxes, so they pay their share

Rebuttal: They do pay most federal income tax, because they get a huge share of income. But much of their wealth growth is never taxed as income, and payroll taxes hit workers harder.

Sources: IRS SOI, SSA

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The deficit is caused by social spending

Rebuttal: Spending is part of it. But corporate tax receipts fell sharply and interest costs rose. Revenue choices matter.

Sources: CBO

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Low unemployment means workers have nothing to complain about

Rebuttal: Unemployment is rising, not low, at 4.2%. And millions are underemployed or falling behind prices.

Sources: BLS

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Workplace deaths are just accidents

Rebuttal: Many are preventable with training, staffing and enforcement. Unions and safety rules reduce deaths.

Sources: BLS, OSHA

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Inflation is over

Rebuttal: Core inflation cooled to 2.4%, but overall prices rose 3.4% through August 2026, and power bills rose 3.8%.

Sources: BLS CPI Aug 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Electricity prices are rising because of green energy

Rebuttal: Many factors drive power bills, including fuel costs, grid upgrades and data-center demand. Prices rose 3.8% over the year to August 2026.

Sources: BLS CPI, EIA

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The poor are poor because they don't work

Rebuttal: Many poor adults work, and BLS counts 4.5 million who want more hours and can't get them. Low pay and costs, not laziness, drive poverty.

Sources: BLS, Census

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Unions only help public workers

Rebuttal: Public-sector density is higher, 32.9%. But private-sector union members also earn more, and private-sector organizing is growing in places like auto and retail.

Sources: BLS 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Black workers have the same opportunities

Rebuttal: Black unemployment was 7.0% in September 2026, well above the national 4.2%. Gaps persist.

Sources: BLS Sept 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Public data can't change anything

Rebuttal: Census data on child poverty helped make the case for the expanded tax credit. Data shapes policy when people organize around it.

Sources: Census SPM

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Karl cherry-picks numbers

Rebuttal: Karl cites official sources and admits good news: record income, falling overdoses, lower homelessness. Then he shows who's left behind.

Sources: Karl's standard

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Statistics can say anything

Rebuttal: Bad statistics can mislead, true. That's why Karl names the agency, the year and what's measured. Honest numbers win arguments.

Sources: Karl's standard

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Cutting federal statistics saves taxpayer money

Rebuttal: Statistical agencies cost little compared with the decisions they inform. Losing data makes policy blind.

Sources: Federal budget data

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Economic growth helps everyone equally

Rebuttal: Growth helps many. But Fed data show the top 1% gained wealth share while the bottom half stayed at 2.5%.

Sources: Federal Reserve DFA

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana is poor because of its people

Rebuttal: Louisiana's people work hard in oil, ports, fishing and care. Policy choices, like no state minimum wage and tax breaks for industry, keep wages low.

Sources: DOL, Census

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The debt means we can't afford public programs

Rebuttal: We found money for tax cuts and interest payments. Affordability is about priorities.

Sources: CBO

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Data doesn't matter to voters

Rebuttal: People trust numbers they can check. A sourced fact from the Census beats a slogan in a debate.

Sources: Karl's standard

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
34.5 million Americans lived in poverty in 2025, an official rate of 10.2%

The rate fell slightly. Still, tens of millions live below a poverty line set far below real living costs.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Income, Poverty and Health Insurance 2025 (Sept. 2026)

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Supplemental Poverty Measure was 13.1% in 2025

Counting taxes, benefits and costs like medical bills, about one in eight people were poor.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Real median household income reached $87,460 in 2025, the highest on record

Good news for the middle. But medians hide how much wealth piles up at the very top.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of poverty in 2025

The single most effective anti-poverty program in the country is public and universal.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Supplemental Poverty Measure 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The official child poverty rate fell to 13.4% in 2025, a historic low

Progress is possible. Policy choices decide how fast.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Child poverty under the Supplemental Poverty Measure fell to 5.2% in 2021, then rose to 12.4% in 2022

The expanded Child Tax Credit cut child poverty to a record low. When Congress let it expire, child poverty more than doubled.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Women working full time, year round earned 83.9% of what men earned in 2025

Up from 80.6% in 2024. A gap still costs women hundreds of thousands over a career.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
26.7 million people, 7.9%, were uninsured for all of 2025

Before most 2025 Medicaid cuts and after subsidies expired. The number is expected to rise.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The top 1% held about 31.6% of U.S. household wealth in early 2026

Their share rose from about 31% at the end of 2024.

Source: Federal Reserve, Distributional Financial Accounts (Q1 2026)

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The bottom 50% of households held about 2.5% of U.S. household wealth in early 2026

Half the country shares a sliver. Wealth isn't trickling down.

Source: Federal Reserve, Distributional Financial Accounts (Q1 2026)

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
CBO estimated the 2025 budget law reduces resources for the lowest-income 10% of households by about $1,200 a year on average

Mostly from cuts to Medicaid and SNAP. That's about 3% of their income.

Source: Congressional Budget Office, 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
CBO estimated the 2025 budget law increases resources for the top 10% of households by about $13,600 a year on average

Tax cuts flow up. Program cuts flow down.

Source: Congressional Budget Office, 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Corporate income tax receipts fell 23% in the first ten months of fiscal 2026, to $298 billion

New write-offs from the 2025 law cut corporate taxes while individual income tax receipts rose 7%.

Source: Congressional Budget Office, Monthly Budget Review, July 2026 (preliminary)

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Net interest on the public debt reached $963 billion in the first ten months of fiscal 2026, up 14%

That's more than the $763 billion spent on the military over the same period.

Source: Congressional Budget Office, Monthly Budget Review, July 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The federal deficit was $1.8 trillion in the first ten months of fiscal 2026

Up $169 billion from the year before. Tax cuts at the top widen the gap.

Source: Congressional Budget Office, Monthly Budget Review, July 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Customs duties, including tariffs, brought in $154 billion in the first ten months of fiscal 2026

Tariffs are taxes paid by importers and often passed on to consumers.

Source: Congressional Budget Office, Monthly Budget Review, July 2026 (preliminary)

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Employers added just 29,000 jobs in September 2026, and unemployment rose to 4.2%

The highest unemployment rate since 2021. About 7.1 million people were out of work.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employment Situation, Oct. 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Black unemployment rate rose to 7.0% in September 2026

Black workers are often the first hit when the economy weakens.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Sept. 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
1.9 million people were long-term unemployed in September 2026, 27.1% of all unemployed

More than a quarter of jobless workers have been looking for six months or more.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Sept. 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
4.5 million people worked part time for economic reasons in September 2026

They want full-time work and can't get it.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Sept. 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Average hourly earnings rose 3.0% over the year to September 2026

Consumer prices rose 3.4% over the year to August. Real pay is slipping.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Sept. 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Consumer prices rose 3.4% over the 12 months ending August 2026

Electricity rose 3.8%. Inflation eats paychecks that aren't protected by contracts.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI, Aug. 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Electricity prices rose 3.8% over the year to August 2026

Power bills outpaced overall inflation. Rising demand, including from data centers, is one pressure analysts point to.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI, Aug. 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
14.7 million wage and salary workers were union members in 2025, a rate of 10.0%

Membership held steady despite fierce employer opposition.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Union Members 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Union members had median weekly earnings of $1,404 in 2025, vs. $1,174 for nonunion workers

About $230 more a week. Unions raise pay.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Union Members 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The private-sector union membership rate was 5.9% in 2025; the public-sector rate was 32.9%

Private-sector workers face the toughest anti-union campaigns.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
There were 5,070 fatal work injuries in 2024, one every 104 minutes

Deaths fell 4% from 2023. Many were preventable.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries 2024

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
1,229 Hispanic or Latino workers died from work injuries in 2024; 68.5% were foreign-born

Immigrant workers carry some of the most dangerous jobs.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, CFOI 2024

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Transportation incidents caused 38.2% of fatal work injuries in 2024

Drivers and delivery workers face deadly roads every shift.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, CFOI 2024

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
470 workers were killed by homicide on the job in 2024

Workplace violence is a safety issue employers must address.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, CFOI 2024

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
U.S. life expectancy reached 79.0 years in 2024, a record high

Mainly due to falling overdose and COVID deaths. Peer nations still live longer.

Source: CDC National Center for Health Statistics, Jan. 2026

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
79,384 people died of drug overdoses in 2024, and the overdose death rate fell 26.2%

The largest decline ever recorded. Treatment and naloxone work.

Source: CDC National Center for Health Statistics

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Suicide became the 10th leading cause of death in 2024

Mental health care access saves lives.

Source: CDC National Center for Health Statistics

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
U.S. household debt totaled $18.8 trillion in the second quarter of 2026

Families are carrying heavy debt loads.

Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Household Debt and Credit Report

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Credit card balances reached $1.263 trillion in the second quarter of 2026

Many families use credit cards to cover basics.

Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Student loan balances totaled $1.651 trillion in the second quarter of 2026

Education debt weighs on a generation.

Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Auto loan balances reached $1.713 trillion in the second quarter of 2026

People borrow heavily just to get to work.

Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
About 745,652 people were homeless on a single night in January 2025, down 3.4% from 2024

The first decline since 2016. Family homelessness fell 11%.

Source: HUD, 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Chronic homelessness reached a record 155,750 people in 2025

The longest-suffering are still falling through.

Source: HUD, 2025 AHAR

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana's poverty rate was 19.7% for 2023–2025, the highest in the nation

Nearly double the U.S. rate. Mississippi was second at 17.6%.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau (three-year average)

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The USDA ended its annual Household Food Security survey in 2025, making the 2024 report the last

The survey had run for about 30 years under both parties. There will be no 2025 count.

Source: USDA announcement, Sept. 2025; final report Dec. 2025

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
47.9 million people lived in food-insecure households in 2024, 13.7% of households

That included 18.4% of households with children. The government stopped counting after this report.

Source: USDA Economic Research Service, final report (Dec. 2025)

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
NOAA logged 27 billion-dollar weather and climate disasters in 2024, costing about $183 billion

NOAA retired the database in 2025. The storms didn't stop.

Source: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The federal tipped minimum wage has been $2.13 an hour since 1991

Thirty-five years without a raise.

Source: U.S. Department of Labor

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Five states, including Louisiana, have no state minimum wage law

Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina and Tennessee rely on the $7.25 federal floor.

Source: U.S. Department of Labor

title: Claude Drop: publicdata-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Social Security taxable wage cap is $184,500 in 2026

Wages above the cap pay no Social Security tax. High earners stop paying early in the year.

Source: Social Security Administration
